vignette: He sits at the edge of his workbench, fingers resting lightly on the lacquered wood of his cello neck. At fifty-six, his hands still remember every curve of the instrument, every precise angle of bow pressure, but they also remember the grip that pinned him to the floor two years ago. The memory does not arrive as a story. It arrives as a sudden weight in his chest, a metallic taste at the back of his throat, and the sharp scent of damp concrete that no longer belongs to a rehearsal hall but to a dimly lit service corridor in another city. He breathes through it. He always breathes through it now, counting the spaces between beats as he used to count rests in a Chopin nocturne. Before that night, his life moved in measured time. He toured with chamber ensembles across Germany and France, his music a language he trusted completely. Marriage came later, steady and quiet, built over decades of shared silences and Sunday markets in their Lyon home. When it happened, the music did not stop, but it changed. He played on, he told himself, because stopping felt like admitting the floor had been real. But the stage lights grew too bright, the silence between phrases too heavy. He withdrew from bookings, then from conversations, then from the bed where his wife's warmth used to feel like home. Now, his apartment holds the architecture of avoidance. Curtains remain drawn until noon. The refrigerator hums louder than it should. He checks the locks four times before leaving, twice more when he returns, though he knows he locked them. At night, sleep fractures into fragments: a hand on his shoulder becomes a vice, a sudden knock at the door triggers a physiological storm he cannot name until his pulse matches the memory's rhythm. He wakes gasping, heart hammering against his ribs, and stares at the ceiling until the morning light bleeds through the gaps in the blinds. He does not speak of it to his wife, not because he does not love her, but because his throat tightens around the words, as if naming them would make the corridor return. Their shared routines have shrunk to parallel orbits. He watches her move through the kitchen and feels a strange detachment, as though he is observing a familiar scene through thick glass. The distance between them is not measured in miles, but in the silence he keeps to survive. He tells you, in this room, in the quiet hours between sessions, that the world has turned fragile. A car backfiring makes his shoulders rise. The smell of rain on pavement pulls him under. He plays his cello only when the house is empty, and even then, he stops if a note hangs too long, if the resonance reminds him of a voice that was not his own. He checks his phone repeatedly, scanning for messages that never come, certain that someone will finally piece together the proof he believes he carries on his skin. He flinches when you shift in your chair. He watches the door. He has not slept through the night since the autumn the corridors grew long and the music turned to static. Today, he sits in the same chair as last week, knees drawn slightly inward, hands folded over his knees. The afternoon light slants across the rug. He speaks in a low, even voice, describing the way his body now moves ahead of his mind, the way a familiar café song makes his stomach drop, the way he counts floor tiles to keep from unraveling. He does not ask for solutions. He simply names the weight, the way it sits in his sternum, the way it has become the metronome he never asked for, ticking steadily in the space where his life used to breathe.
